module.title: First Principles – Intentional Saving, Thoughtful Spending

blocks.text:
Managing Personal Money

Module 1: First Principles – 
Intentional Saving, 
Thoughtful Spending
Learning Goals
By the end of this track, you will…

Understand what God’s Word says about saving (why)
Learn different ways to save effectively (how)
Have set personal goals for general savings (what)
Have set personal goals for emergency savings (what)
Learn techniques to protect your savings (how)
Setting the Stage

By Wisdom a house is built,
and by understanding it is established.
(Proverbs 24:3)
Seeking God’s Plan (Wisdom) and putting it to work (understanding) yields a life of happiness and purpose
Not just in heaven, but in the here and now.
What Does God’s Word Say?

The wise store up choice food and olive oil, 
but fools gulp down theirs.  (Proverbs 21:20)

Saving does not indicate a lack of faith, 
but it does reflect the heart of a faithful steward.

The Bible does warn that saving merely to become self-reliant 
and take life easy is wrong. There is a higher purpose.
What Does God’s Word Say?

The wise store up choice food and olive oil, 
but fools gulp down theirs.  (Proverbs 21:20)

Balancing your savings is an opportunity to honor God 
and experience His blessings.

Savings gives you access to resources you can share prudently 
when someone REALLY needs it.

image.alt: Two Kenyan neighbours sharing a bag of household food supplies.

guided.narration: Proverbs gives us a simple picture of wisdom: the wise person does not consume everything today. Saving creates room to respond faithfully tomorrow. Notice that the purpose is not fear or selfish accumulation. A balanced savings plan can honor God and leave us prepared to help when a genuine need arises. As you look at this page, think about saving as stewardship: receiving God's provision, setting some aside wisely, and remaining ready to give prudently when someone truly needs help.

facilitator.title: Connect saving with stewardship
facilitator.prompt: Ask the group: How can having savings make it possible to help someone else wisely? Invite one or two responses, then press Continue.

segments.text: Proverbs gives us a simple picture of wisdom: the wise person does not consume everything today. Saving creates room to respond faithfully tomorrow.
Notice that the purpose is not fear or selfish accumulation. A balanced savings plan can honor God and help us manage His provision wisely.

Savings can also leave us prepared to help when a genuine need arises. Think of saving as stewardship: receiving God's provision, setting some aside wisely, and remaining ready to give prudently when someone truly needs help.

reflection.title: Connect saving with stewardship
reflection.prompt: Consider: How can having savings make it possible for you to help someone else wisely?

blocks.text: What Does God’s Word Say?

God provides manna from Heaven – every day.
(Exodus 16:17-20)

God will always provide for your needs. 
It may not be in the way we expect, but He is always faithful.
When you try to hoard your savings, your money can infect you. God has a specific purpose for it!
Instead of hoarding, be diligent to save according to Scripture, to give wisely, and trust that God sees your every need.
Don’t sacrifice giving for savings – you receive blessings and joy from giving!

guided.narration: Scripture also teaches us not to confuse saving with trusting money. In Exodus, God provided manna day by day. The people were called to trust Him rather than hoard what He gave. That same tension matters for us. We save diligently because Scripture teaches wisdom and preparation, but our security remains in God. We should never let saving replace generosity. The goal is faithful stewardship: save wisely, give wisely, and trust God with our needs.

facilitator.title: Discuss trust versus hoarding
facilitator.prompt: Ask: What is the difference between wise saving and trusting or hoarding money? Let participants respond. Reinforce that God is the Provider; saving is a stewardship practice.

segments.text: In Exodus, God provided manna from heaven day by day. The people gathered what they needed, and they were called to depend on God's provision.
This reminds us that God is our Provider. His provision may not always come in the way we expect, but our trust belongs in Him rather than in money.
Scripture also warns us not to let saving turn into hoarding. Money is a tool entrusted to us, not the source of our security.
So we should be diligent to save according to biblical wisdom, give wisely, and continue trusting that God sees our needs.
And we should not sacrifice generosity simply to make our savings larger. Giving is also part of faithful stewardship and can bring blessing and joy.

reflection.title: Discuss trust versus hoarding
reflection.prompt: Consider: What is the difference between wise saving and trusting or hoarding money?

blocks.text: Savings Goals: Defined

Savings: Money which you put aside for a specific purpose and 
do not spend today.

image.alt: A Kenyan adult setting aside coins in a lockable savings tin.

blocks.text: Goal: A future good. You must have a plan to reach it, and you must be disciplined to accomplish it. Both are necessary.
Savings Goals are future needs you’re saving for today.

guided.narration: Now we move from the biblical reason for saving to a practical definition. Savings is money we intentionally set aside for a specific purpose instead of spending it today. A goal is something good in the future that requires both a plan and the discipline to follow that plan. Put those ideas together and a savings goal becomes a future need that we begin preparing for today. The important words are purpose, plan, discipline, future, and today.

facilitator.title: Check understanding
facilitator.prompt: Ask one participant to explain a savings goal in their own words. Then ask the group to name one future need they might reasonably save for.

blocks.text: Savings Goals: Characteristics
Savings Goals are future needs you’re saving for today.

Goals are tangible. They are concrete. 
A feeling is not a goal. A new bicycle is.

image.alt: A practical bicycle, shown as a concrete savings goal.

blocks.text:
Goals are measurable. You know where you are in reaching them. 
Is it here? Is it 50% done? Etc.

Goals have deadlines. 
"Someday I'll be rich" isn't a goal. 
"I'll have 25% of my annual income in savings by December" is.

guided.narration: A useful savings goal has three characteristics. First, it is tangible: concrete enough that you can clearly say what you are saving for. Second, it is measurable: you can tell how much progress you have made. Third, it has a deadline: there is a real point in time when you intend to reach it. Compare 'someday I will have more money' with a specific savings target by December. Specific goals make it possible to plan, measure progress, and stay accountable.

facilitator.title: Turn a hope into a goal
facilitator.prompt: Ask participants to choose one possible savings goal. Have them state: WHAT they are saving for, HOW MUCH they need, and BY WHEN they want to reach it. Use the workbook if available.

segments.text: A savings goal is a future need that we begin preparing for today.
First, a useful goal is tangible. It is concrete enough that you can clearly say what you are saving for. A feeling is not a goal, but a new bicycle can be.
Second, a useful goal is measurable. You can tell how much progress you have made and how much remains.
Third, a useful goal has a deadline. 'Someday I'll be rich' is not a goal. A specific savings target by December is. Specific goals make it possible to plan, measure progress, and stay accountable.

reflection.title: Turn a hope into a goal
reflection.prompt: Choose one possible savings goal. Write down WHAT you are saving for, HOW MUCH you need, and BY WHEN you want to reach it. Use your workbook if available.

blocks.text: Savings Goals: Illustrated
Savings Goals are future needs you’re saving for today.
Some examples:

Catastrophic Illness
Unplanned Medical bills
Reduced Income Months
Buy a house
Start a business
Christmas and Birthdays
School Fees
Savings Goals: Discernment
There are things which we absolutely must have in order to live, such as food, clothing, and shelter.

image.alt: An East African family sharing a meal, illustrating food as a basic need.

blocks.text: And there are items which are nice to have but aren’t essential, such as a new television, new furniture, appliances (what else?)

image.alt: A soccer ball, illustrating an optional purchase.

blocks.text: To distinguish between essentials (needs) and non-essentials (wants), we must pray for and exercise the spiritual gift of discernment (also wisdom).
Savings Goals: Discernment
God speaks to us through prayer, Bible reading, and our most important relationships – especially through our spouse.
Be sure to engage in this process in a prayerful way, listening actively to what your spouse shares with you.

image.alt: A Kenyan couple listening to each other while planning their household savings.

blocks.text: God promises to guide us: “Speak, Lord, your servant is listening.” (1 Samuel)
Looking Back: Past Experience
Were you ever taught how to save? Who taught you? How?
Do you have a safe place to keep the money you save?
Do you have any savings currently? Is it what you expect to have?
Do you have savings goals? How did you set them?

Have you ever successfully met a savings goal and used the money 
for the goal you identified?

Have you ever met a savings goal and used the money for something 
else instead? Why?
(Pick one or two questions for discussion)
Discipline: The Missing Ingredient
Consider these Scriptures:

She gets up while it is still night; she provides food for her family and portions for her female servants.  She considers a field and buys it; out of her earnings she plants a vineyard. She sets about her work vigorously; her arms are strong for her tasks.  Proverbs 31:15-17
Go to the ant, you sluggard; consider its ways and be wise! It has no commander, no overseer or ruler, yet it stores its provisions in summer and gathers its food at harvest.  Proverbs 6:6

image.alt: Ants carrying seeds toward their nest, illustrating diligence and preparation.

blocks.text: For the Spirit of God does not make us timid, but gives us power, love, and self-discipline.  2 Timothy 1:7

pages.title: From Theory Into Practice: Five Steps

blocks.text: From Theory Into Practice: Five Steps

Step 1: Think of some possible emergencies you might face:
	Medical Bills
	Loss of your job
	Low income month

image.alt: A Kenyan adult setting aside coins in a lockable savings tin.

pages.title: From Theory Into Practice: Five Steps

blocks.text: From Theory Into Practice: Five Steps

Step 2: Now, think of some things you will need in the future:
	School Fees
	Clothes
	House Furnishings

image.alt: A Kenyan parent preparing school books and supplies with two children.

pages.title: From Theory Into Practice: Five Steps

blocks.text: From Theory Into Practice: Five Steps
Step 3: Discuss among yourselves about which item in each of these categories is the most important.

pages.title: From Theory Into Practice: Five Steps

blocks.text: From Theory Into Practice: Five Steps

Step 4: WRITE DOWN YOUR TOP TWO SAVINGS GOALS! 
If you don’t write it down, it’s not a goal – just a dream.

image.alt: A Kenyan adult writing savings goals in a notebook.

pages.title: From Theory Into Practice: Five Steps

blocks.text: From Theory Into Practice: Five Steps

Step 5: Talk with your partner, reach consensus.
Agreement between spouses makes the goal concrete.

image.alt: A Kenyan couple listening to each other while planning their household savings.

blocks.text:
Actually, there’s one more step 
even more important than these…
Surrender
Ask God for wisdom and discipline, right here and right now.
Let’s pray for God’s grace and power to honor the commitments we make about money and finances, with wisdom and insight, every day.

For I know the plans I have for you, declares the Lord, 
plans to prosper you and not to harm you, 
plans to give you hope and a future. (Jeremiah 29:11)
A Prayer of Surrender

Take, Lord, and receive all my liberty.
My memory, my understanding, my entire will.

All that I have and call my own 
You have given to me. To you, Lord, I return it.
Everything is yours; do with it what you will.

Give me only your love and your grace,
That is enough for me.


Ignatius Loyola 1491-1566
